extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Popular Science Monthly — educated lay readers and specialists (botanists, mathematicians, naturalists, and technologists)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and standards for reviewing and producing scientific books, periodicals, and technical apparatus as discussed in a Popular Science Monthly 'Literary Notices' section. Covers expectations for botanical floras, mathematical journals, scientific essays, and telephonic transmitters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical arrangement and compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: The working botanist will first notice the excellent mechanical arrangement of the flora, especially its compactness as compared with former works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attain compactness partly by conciseness of description but mainly by omission of extended synonymy; provide synonymy separately (e.g., in a bibliographical index) so the main work remains compact and usable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness of descriptive entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Conciseness of description: brief descriptions that seize and point out distinctive characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions should be concise yet sufficient to identify species; avoid unnecessary verbosity while ensuring distinctive characters are clear to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission (and separate treatment) of extended synonymy
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of extended synonymy in the main flora to improve compactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve full synonymy in a separate bibliographical index (as by Sereno Watson) so the flora is compact for most users while exhaustive references remain available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic versus specific description discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The generic description should give characters which cover every species, while the specific description should not repeat any of the generic characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure hierarchy: give broad, covering characters in the genus entry and reserve species entries for characters not already covered by the genus; failure to observe this is tedious for users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and organization of large genera
rubrics_metrics.description: Large genera should be grouped in subgenera, sections, and subsections, each briefly defined by prominent characters common to all members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where large genera exist, subdivide into meaningful named subgenera and further sections so that the systematic botanist can navigate complexity without redundant descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of keys for audience level
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial keys to genera or species are convenient in elementary works but the systematic flora may prefer subgenera/groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use keys for educational/elementary works to aid identification; in advanced systematic treatments prefer taxonomic grouping (subgenera, sections) that reflect the author's perception of essential relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative perception and distinctive-character emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good flora is marked by the author's keen perception which seizes upon and points out the distinctive characters and broad views of genera and species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should demonstrate experience and judgment so that their treatments reflect reliable, authoritative decisions about distinguishing characters and generic limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and completeness relative to available material
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Flora of North America' should be published when sufficient material exists to present a fairly complete record; timing matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay or suspend publication if field knowledge is rapidly changing until sufficient exploration and collections allow a more complete and enduring work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodical frequency and scale expectations (mathematical journal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The American Journal of Mathematics is to appear quarterly (or nearly so), each volume containing about 384 quarto pages (four numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set and communicate realistic frequency and size for a scholarly periodical so subscribers and libraries can assess commitment and content capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary content objective for a specialist journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary object: the publication of original mathematical investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specialist journal should prioritize original research while also including concise abstracts of important subjects and critical/bibliographical notices to aid the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary contents for scholarly usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to original investigations, include concise abstracts, critical and bibliographical notices, and reviews of important publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplementary material increases accessibility of difficult or obscure work and situates new papers in the broader literature for students and researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience match and accessibility (journal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematical periodical is not popular and will be unintelligible to non-mathematical readers; it is designed chiefly as a medium between American mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that specialist journals target a technical audience; encourage support (subscriptions, gifts to libraries) from public-spirited patrons to sustain high-level scholarship that serves students and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and unity of a collected volume
rubrics_metrics.description: A volume composed of essays should avoid appearing as a slightly heterogeneous mixture; it should have a consistent raison d'etre or coherent arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assembling essays into a book, ensure the selection and ordering create a coherent whole; avoid inserting loosely-related pieces merely to give a title-based justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced exposition of familiar topics
rubrics_metrics.description: On well-worn topics (e.g., tropical nature) avoid undue exaggeration; present facts well-arranged and vividly to bring salient points to readers without theatrical glamour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for clear, measured presentation that informs untraveled or non-specialist readers without sensationalizing; arrange and illustrate facts to highlight important differences and causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific argument: parsimony and careful reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific conclusions should be carefully reasoned and prefer simpler explanations where adequate (e.g., Wallace argues many color phenomena are explained by natural selection rather than sexual selection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate hypotheses for explanatory power and parsimony; show how natural selection can account for phenomena before invoking additional mechanisms; avoid unscientific or gratuitous language when advancing speculative extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and typology as explanatory tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify phenomena into clear categories (Wallace: protective colors, warning colors, sexual colors, and typical colors) to clarify causes and functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pragmatic typologies to analyze biological traits, attributing functions (e.g., concealment, warning, recognition) and explaining how selection may act differently on sexes or roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmitter sensitivity and fidelity (telephone apparatus)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful transmitter (microphone) exhibits amazing sensitiveness to sound and power of conveying it with the utmost fidelity; picks up sounds otherwise inaudible and conveys them to great distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations of performance: tiny touches, brush strokes, heartbeat or watch-tick transmitted clearly and magnified; ability to represent very small mechanical inputs as audible signals is a key performance metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct pickup by the transmitter (device architecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The microphone's peculiarity is that sounds are taken up directly by the 'transmitter' (the mercurialized carbon plugs or selenium response) rather than indirectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design receivers/transmitters to convert acoustic agitation into changes in electrical conductivity at the site of the transmitter so the weakest mechanical vibrations modulate current effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material and configuration innovation (transmitter design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of porous charcoal infiltrated with metallic mercury arranged as a series of plugs in a small glass tube (mercurialized carbon transmitter) produced greatly augmented sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with finely-divided conducting materials, imperfect/broken contacts, and light-sensitive elements (selenium) to exploit changes in conductivity under mechanical or optical agitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulus-dependent conductivity behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Pieces of carbon barely touching will not pass current, but when the molecules are agitated by sound-waves they transmit electricity freely; similar effects occur under light exposure for selenium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and evaluate components that change conductivity responsively to the intended stimulus (sound or light), ensuring that quiet/rest states do not pass current while agitated states do — this dynamic is central to sensitivity.
